free_text.inst.v2.D8: I read the plain-words page first, then answered from what is actually documented about her life. The two don't line up well. 'About you' calls the temperament quick-minded, talkative, at home with words, numbers and dealing - that is not the woman of the record: she was famously plain-spoken but sparing with words, ran no trade or ledger, and is remembered for silence and manual work among the dying, not dealing. The 'matters that read well' list includes marriage and partnerships and children and learning - she took vows of poverty and chastity at eighteen, never married, and had no children; a reading that scores those as favourable is simply describing a life she did not have. Where it happened to land close to true was the 'unusual for this chart' line about being unusually positive on time away from home and living far from your birthplace - she left Skopje at eighteen and spent the rest of her sixty-nine remaining years in Ireland and then India, and by every account that departure and that distance were the making of her vocation, not a hardship. But the same sentence also calls her unusually positive about her father, and the record says the opposite: he died suddenly when she was about eight, and the family's fortunes did not stay steady afterward. The reading also has nothing at all to say about the two things her real biography is actually known for - founding the Missionaries of Charity and the nearly five-decade private crisis of faith disclosed only after her death in her own letters - because the plain-words page is generic enough to fit almost anyone and never touches anything that specific. One hit, several plain misses, and total silence on what actually defined her.

notes: Answered from the documented public biography of Mother Teresa (Anjeze Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, b. 26 Aug 1910 Skopje, d. 5 Sep 1997 Calcutta), reading the engine's plain-reading text first (contaminated arm). Marriage/children/career-as-paid-work/personal-wealth questions do not apply to a nun under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience: A16=not_earning, A20=none, A21=never, A22=none, A23=none, A24=never_married, A25 omitted (never married), A26/A27/A29=na, A28=none. C1 (spending), C7 (married life), C9 (children), C10 (ears/throat), C11 (inheritance) are genuinely non-applicable to her life story; I picked the least-wrong option at confidence 1 in each case and flag them here rather than let a forced choice read as real signal. A10=died_early: her father died in 1919 when she was about eight (matches the well-documented biographical fact the study is testing against), and the family's fortunes worsened afterward, hence A11=reversal rather than steady. A13=close despite the family being cut off physically for decades: she remained emotionally close to her mother and sister Age by letter until Albania's communist border closures around 1946 ended contact before either woman died; I did not mark this 'distant' because the estrangement was external circumstance, not relationship breakdown. A31=extended is a judgment call flagged explicitly: there is no record of clinical diagnosis or psychiatric treatment, but her own letters (published 2007, 'Come Be My Light') document a nearly 50-year documented spiritual darkness/sense of abandonment by God that by her own description was a source of real and sustained anguish - I answered 'extended' to reflect the honest documented experience rather than 'no', which would erase it, but this is spiritual desolation, not a psychiatric diagnosis. A7 (sickly as a child) and A34 (extended institutional time, from repeated hospitalizations in 1983/1989/1991/1996-97) are drawn from generally repeated biographical claims rather than a single primary source and are held with lower confidence than the father's-death and vow-of-poverty facts. B3 (age guessed older) and B5 (born at home) are weakly supported inferences from the era/region and her photographed appearance, not firmly documented facts. A36 has no meaningful answer for a subject who died in 1997 and is omitted rather than guessed. D1/D2/D3 all point to 'plain_reading' because that is the only chapter the study exposed in this arm; within it, the temperament line and the marriage/children entries are flatly contradicted by the record (D1), the 'unusually positive about time away from home / living far from your birthplace' claim is a specific, non-generic hit (D2), and the bulk of the 'matters that read well/hard' lists are Barnum-generic (D3). D4 lists every chapter this arm was never shown.
